adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — [P1, confidence 75] The equal `return 200;` priorities of DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider make a multi-provider classpath select whichever service resource enumeration happens first instead of rejecting the ambiguous deployment, so packaging order selects a different crypto integration with no configuration change.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order() = 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. The diff shows the detection logic sorts by order in descending order and picks the first one. When multiple providers have the same order (200), the selection becomes non-deterministic based on ServiceLoader enumeration order. However, this is by design - these three providers are meant to be mutually exclusive (you use either default BC, Elytron, or FIPS). The new AuthzClientCryptoProvider with order 100 is a fallback. This is an architectural concern worth discussing but not a bug - the system previously threw an exception for multiple providers, now it selects by order. The equal priorities for the main providers could be intentional (expecting only one to be present).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — [P1, confidence 75] `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` permanently installs the authz-only provider into CryptoIntegration's process-global singleton when the authorization client initializes before a fuller provider is visible, so later common-crypto consumers hit the provider's `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.");` methods despite having their own provider on a different classloader.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. Looking at the diff: 1) CryptoIntegration.init() in AuthzClient.create() uses AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader() to initialize the crypto provider. 2) CryptoIntegration.java shows detectProvider() now selects the provider with highest order() value. 3) AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() returning 100, while DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. 4) CryptoIntegration uses a static singleton pattern - once initialized, the provider is set globally. If AuthzClient.create() is called first with a classloader that only sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100), and later code expects a full provider (order 200) but uses a different classloader, the singleton is already set to the limited provider. The AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods. This is a real initialization order bug where the limited provider could be permanently installed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:47 — [confidence:100][severity:P1] `AuthzClientCryptoProvider prov = new AuthzClientCryptoProvider();` bypasses `AuthzClient.create` and ServiceLoader selection, so a broken `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` registration path leaves authorization-client ECDSA flows unconfigured while every added test passes.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the test bypasses CryptoIntegration.init() and therefore doesn't test the real registration path. However, the test's purpose is to unit test the ECDSACryptoProvider implementation (ASN1 encoding/decoding), not to test the ServiceLoader registration. The test directly instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider to test its ECDSA conversion methods, which is a valid unit testing approach. The CryptoIntegration.init() call in AuthzClient.create() is a separate concern - it initializes the crypto provider for runtime use. The test is correctly testing the crypto implementation itself. The finding mischaracterizes what the test is meant to verify.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:54 — [confidence:75][severity:P1] `byte[] asn1Des = prov.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rsConcat, algorithm.getSignatureLength());` is validated only by the same provider's decoder at line 55, so a mutually compatible non-DER encoder/decoder defect keeps the suite green while an external JWT verifier rejects the produced signature.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test design limitation in the new ECDSAAlgorithmTest. Looking at lines 51-56, the test converts ASN1 DER to concatenated RS using the provider's decoder, then converts back using the encoder, then decodes again - but only asserts that rsConcat equals rsConcat2. This is a round-trip test within the same implementation. The test doesn't verify against an external reference or the original 'sign' bytes. While this is a valid concern about test coverage for newly added crypto code, it's not a bug - the implementation could still be correct. The finding is specific and grounded in the diff, pointing to a real gap in test validation for security-critical cryptographic code.
